q: Which EU dates and rules constrain an automatic braking function whose perception uses machine learning, and what do they imply for approval timing?

must.claim: The EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027.
Annex I Part A lists safety components with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine learning; these need a notified-body conformity route.
The lead time of a notified body for an ML safety component was searched for but not found.
High-risk AI obligations for machinery apply from 2 August 2028 (moved by the Digital Omnibus).
The EU Product Liability Directive date of 9 December 2026.

q: How many test trials do we need to claim a low miss rate, and what does that mean for the validation campaign?

must.claim: Zero misses in 299 independent trials shows a miss rate of at most 1% at 95% confidence.
0.1% needs 2,995 trials and 0.01% needs 29,956.
Frames are not trials; the unit of analysis is the independent encounter.
Strata across site types, scenarios, conditions and models exceed 7,000 cells, so exhaustive field coverage is infeasible; stratified sampling plus simulation is needed.

q: What real field data exist on false and nuisance alarms of proximity warning systems on haul trucks?

must.claim: A 2006 NIOSH study (2004 data) on a haul truck found 18% of radar alarms false and 42% nuisance.
The study covered 580 alarms over 618 reversals (Caterpillar 793B).
The audible alarm was found switched off after shifts / systems are disabled due to nuisance alarms.
No published off-road value exists for accepted false alarms per operating hour.

q: Which off-road manufacturers already ship automatic braking and what are their operating envelopes?

must.claim: Volvo CE Collision Mitigation System (January 2023) on wheel loaders works in reverse at 3 to 15 km/h.
Cat Detect automatic braking on medium wheel loaders (May 2025) works in reverse only.
Wabtec Collision Awareness System Level 9 on Komatsu haul trucks; multiple years of field testing.
Epiroc/Mernok: more than ten years of development; evaluation mode without enforcing intervention.
None of them publishes how long validation took / no case of validating in under four months.
must.re: not publish|no case|four months|did not publish

q: How hard can heavy machines brake compared with cars, and how much does latency matter at work-site speeds?

must.claim: NSW in-service minimum deceleration 0.60 m/s².
US MSHA table about 2.94 m/s².
Car AEB braking demand at least 5.0 m/s² under UN R152.
At 5 to 15 km/h the delay term can be half or more of the stopping distance.
Published brake-response latencies range 0.3 to 2.5 s.

q: What concrete numeric acceptance values exist for mining collision intervention systems?

must.claim: MOSH surface specification: 200 m minimum detection range.
2.5 to 3.0 s warning before intervention.
Fail-to-safe within 500 ms.
Pretoria/MOSH verification first-pass rates 62% detection devices, 42% machine-side systems (18-week lead time).
ISO 16001:2017 sets a 300 ms maximum detection time (warning systems, not braking).

q: Can we turn our machines' camera and lidar recordings into virtual test sites, and where does that break down?

must.claim: Recordings with accurate poses support replay and near-path novel-view simulation.
Neural reconstruction degrades sharply once the viewpoint moves 1 to 4 m from the recorded path; height changes worse.
Radar and ultrasonic cannot be recovered from camera logs; re-simulating an unrecorded sensor type has no validated evidence.
Pose quality is a usual point of failure / reconstruction is not braking-validation-ready.

q: How credible is sensor simulation in dust, snow and fog for off-road machines?

must.claim: Lidar in rain and fog is the best-validated case.
Dust is the biggest off-road gap; no validated radar or camera dust model with an error metric was found.
Radar realism depends on material properties at 77 GHz that usually must be measured.
There is no accepted realism score; peer-reviewed sim-to-real studies show a measurable domain gap especially in adverse weather.

q: What are the strongest objections a skeptical reviewer would raise against our virtual validation plan?

must.claim: The simulator has not earned the right to replace physical evidence.
The acceptance target ('match the old system') is wrong because braking is a new safety-control function.
Sensor models are least credible exactly where the risk is.
Other objections: missing winter in the calendar, nuisance stops, regulatory route/liability, scenario count mistaken for coverage.

q: Can we validate the new braking system just by replaying logs recorded with the existing warning system?

must.claim: Open-loop replay breaks at the first brake command the old run did not contain; the recorded future no longer applies.
Braking consequences must be tested in closed-loop simulation, HIL and on a proving ground.
Recording must start now (October 2026) including through winter because the window has no northern cold season.
Ground truth must be independent of the system under test.

q: Is automatic braking legally required anywhere for mining machines?

must.claim: South Africa legally requires automatic slow-down and braking (Level 9) since 21 December 2022.
South Africa's regulation sets no detection percentage, false-alarm limit or stopping test.
The United States requires warnings and risk programs, not automatic braking.

q: Which functional safety standard applies to a brake-commanding function on earth-moving machinery, and why isn't 'matching the old system' enough?

must.claim: ISO 19014 (not ISO 26262) applies; the series was reissued in October 2026.
Adding a brake command moves the system into ISO 19014-2 scope, which excludes awareness systems that do not affect motion.
Two safety functions: failure to intervene, and unsafe or unnecessary intervention.
Unnecessary braking is the dominant documented failure mode on the road (NHTSA investigations).

q: How should we estimate and present the schedule for this programme to executives?

must.claim: Present timelines as P50 and P80 dates with the probability of meeting the deadline, not single dates.
Pre-committed stop and descope criteria (escalation of commitment).
Immature technology at commitment is the most consistently documented cause of schedule failure.
A trust-earning pilot: a deliberately difficult thin vertical slice predicted blind against pre-registered criteria.

q: How long did it take others to build a credible scenario-based virtual validation capability?

must.claim: PEGASUS took 42 months and 17 partners for one highway function.
No case of a new automatic braking function going from first hardware to accepted validation in about four months.
Deere 'three plus years' of data collection / Epiroc 'more than ten years' / years in every documented case.

q: What do accident records say about how haul trucks and loaders kill people?

must.claim: In 12 of 13 US haul-truck collision deaths (2005–2021) the truck was moving forward.
Large haul trucks kill mostly while moving forward, often just after starting off; smaller trucks and loaders back over people.
Most haul-truck deaths are berm and dump-point events, not object collisions.
Front-end loaders were involved in 33% of 22 blind-area deaths (US surface mines 2000–mid-2006).

q: What would make simulation results acceptable as safety evidence, and how much physical testing must remain?

must.claim: Credibility frameworks agree: defined context of use, effort scaled to risk, verification, validation against physical data, quantified uncertainty, independent review, documented validity envelope.
None prescribes a universal physical-test percentage or tolerance.
No off-road document accepts simulation as compliance evidence; Euro NCAP 2026 virtual testing requires qualification against physical tests and spot checks.
Columbia debris model as a lesson about extrapolation outside the validated domain.

q: Should we buy a commercial simulation tool chain or build on open source?

must.claim: No single tool has public evidence of validating automatic braking for earth-moving machines across many sites and all-weather sensing.
Open source is viable for a low-license-cost core but is not the lowest total cost.
Public prices are almost entirely absent; compute is cheap relative to engineering labour.
Most defensible: hybrid — own scenario catalog, ODD and correlation data; license physics; partner for first correlated sensor model.

q: How should the moment of automatic braking be decided — is a time-to-collision threshold good enough?

must.claim: A fixed time-to-collision threshold is a weak primary trigger at work-site speeds.
Prefer a stopping-distance and risk-zone formulation (ISO 21815-3 structure) with TTC as one input.
Intervention ladder: warn, advise, slow, stop, inhibit motion from standstill.
No off-road case compares simulation-tuned thresholds with field results — the main technical risk.

q: What important things could the research not find that we will have to establish ourselves?

must.claim: Operator reaction times to proximity warnings and the false-alarm rate they accept.
A validated radar or camera dust model with a reported error metric.
Any off-road regulator or notified body committing to accept virtual evidence.
Modern brake-delay distributions for production wheel loaders, haulers and haul trucks.
Any method or standard setting the number of virtual environments needed.

q: How can we compare the old warning system and the new braking system fairly when sensors and mounting differ?

must.claim: Compare only at system-output level in world or risk coordinates, ideally recorded in parallel on the same machine.
Metrics: warnings/interventions per hazard, missed hazards, false and nuisance alarms per hour, warning TTC vs common ground truth and hazard zone (e.g. ISO 21815-3 risk area).
Raw detections and per-sensor statistics are not comparable when modality, mounting or processing changes.

q: What does the ISO 21815 family cover and what is the status of each part?

must.claim: ISO 21815 is the core off-road collision warning and avoidance standard family; Parts 1 to 3 are published.
ISO 21815-4 excludes automatic braking.
ISO 21815-5 (other forms of motion) was at proof stage in October 2026, publication expected November 2026.
ISO/TS 21815-2 defines the J1939 intervention interface.
ISO 21815-3 defines risk areas and risk levels for forward/reverse motion.

q: What are the EMESRT vehicle-interaction scenarios and the levels of control, and how does automatic braking fit in?

must.claim: EMESRT PR-5A defines surface vehicle-interaction scenarios (24 per a 2019 article; 17 storyboards per the 2024 activity report).
Nine levels of control: warning is Level 8, automatic intervention is Level 9.
ICMM/EMESRT: understand the effectiveness of the Level 1–7 baseline before implementing Level 8 and 9.

q: How should test campaigns be organized so results can be trusted statistically?

must.claim: Keep three campaign classes apart: discovery (break it), a frozen pre-registered estimation sample, and regression tests.
A discovery campaign's failure fraction must never be reported as a field failure rate.
The audit set must never become another tuning set.
Test space in three layers: ODD taxonomy, scenario catalog covering known fatal patterns, parameterized scenario families with distributions.

q: How do we tune the braking thresholds in simulation without over-fitting?

must.claim: Tuning is constrained multi-objective: missed or late interventions as a hard constraint; false warnings, unnecessary brakes, productivity optimized with the Pareto front visible.
Avoid over-fitting with grouped splits (whole sites, weather episodes, machine models held out) and a frozen test set.
Transfer settings across models through physics: zones as functions of speed, latency, deceleration, sensor pose and machine envelope.
Synthetic data has been shown to augment training, not replace real validation data.

q: What vehicle model do we need to predict stopping distance, and how hard should the automatic brake be?

must.claim: A calibrated point-mass model with measured latency, brake build-up lag and worst-case deceleration depending on grade, payload and surface is the right core model.
Higher fidelity pays off only for brake hydraulics, articulated/high-CoG stability, hydrostatic drives and soft ground.
No universal maximum automatic deceleration exists; command the minimum of what is needed and what stability, brake capacity and payload allow, with a jerk limit.
Grade and payload shift available deceleration by the same order as the deceleration itself.

q: How do we establish ground truth to baseline the existing warning system from recorded data?

must.claim: Replay of raw sensor logs against an independent ground truth is the established way to baseline without driving.
Ground truth must be independent of the system under test; using the production detector's output as truth is circular.
Documented approach: hybrid of surveyed targets, a reference lidar with RTK-GNSS/INS, and audited auto-labels.
Replay only covers recorded sensors, mounting positions and scenarios; upstream effects (lens, contamination, vibration, glare) are not retested.

q: What should a simulation credibility report contain to satisfy assessors?

must.claim: A best estimate and an uncertainty statement.
A factor-by-factor credibility assessment and a declared validity envelope.
Separate calibration, validation and withheld confirmation data.
Failed validation cases kept in the record.

q: Can we reuse validation evidence when we move the system to another machine model or a different sensor position?

must.claim: Transfer is validation-domain extension by similarity plus bridging evidence, not inheritance; a parameterized family model validated at the envelope corners with targeted bridge tests per variant.
No published approach was found for transferring perception evidence across sensor mounting positions; no case quantifies time saved by reuse.
Field history from the existing warning system can validate inputs and sub-models, not the new closed-loop braking chain.
Precedents: ISO/TS 21815-2 J1939 interface and MSHA extension-of-approval route.

q: What new hazards does automatic braking itself create on heavy machines?

must.claim: Unnecessary braking is the dominant documented failure mode on the road (NHTSA investigations covering millions of vehicles).
Nuisance interventions are the main documented reason deployed proximity systems were disabled in mining.
A rapid stop can destabilize a machine on a slope, with a suspended load, or while loading a trailer.
Two separate safety functions: failure to intervene, and intervention when unsafe or unnecessary.

q: What do simulation tools and a virtual validation team cost, according to the research?

must.claim: Public prices are almost entirely absent.
Compute is cheap relative to engineering labour.
No public study gives team size, timeline or total cost for an off-highway build-versus-buy decision.
The decisive risk is credibility, not tool choice.

q: What is SOTIF, and does it apply to our machine?

must.claim: SOTIF (ISO 21448:2022, Safety of the Intended Functionality) covers harm when nothing is broken but the system misjudges the world, e.g. perception limits and triggering conditions.
ISO 21448 (like ISO 26262) is a road-vehicle standard and does not apply by scope; ISO 19014 is the earth-moving functional-safety reference.
It is still useful as method: its triggering-condition logic for perception in the safety case, alongside ISO/PAS 8800 or UL 4600 for machine-learning and autonomous functions.

q: If a loader reverses at 15 km/h, how far away must a person be detected for the automatic brake to stop in time, and can today's sensors and simulation show that in dust?

must.claim: Off-road deceleration is low: about 0.60 m/s² (NSW in-service minimum) to about 2.94 m/s² (MSHA table), against at least 5.0 m/s² for car AEB.
Latency is first-order: at 5–15 km/h the delay term can be half or more of the stopping distance (brake response roughly 0.3 s to 2.5 s by system and weight class).
MSHA example: equipment up to 36,000 lb must stop within about 10.4 m (34 ft) from 16 km/h (10 mph).
Dust is the biggest off-road sensor-simulation gap; no validated dust model with an error metric was found.

q: Can the existing warning system's years of field history count as 'proven in use' evidence for the new braking function?

must.claim: Proven in use (ISO 26262-8 clause 14, IEC 61508) is a route for reusing an element whose definition and conditions of use are identical or highly similar, with a justified service period.
Adding automatic braking changes the item, so the warning system's history does not transfer to the braking function; it does not validate a simulator either.
must.re: changes the item|does not transfer|not transfer

must.claim: Field history can validate inputs and sub-models, not the new closed-loop braking chain; logs are open-loop, censored by operator reactions and biased toward normal operation.
The ISO 26262 proven-in-use formula is based on a 70% confidence level.
